series.name: Paise Ki Baat
series.tagline: Real money. Real stories. Real consequences.
series.concept: Real money stories told as drama. Not financial advice — just stories that teach through emotion. SIPs, PPF, LIC, EMIs, gold, real estate — every episode is a true-feeling financial story from everyday Indian life told like a friend sharing a lesson over chai.

episodes.title: ₹5000 a Month

slides.text: He earned ₹30,000 a month. No rich parents. No side business. No crypto. At 45, he was worth ₹2 crore.
In 2004, Ravi opened a SIP. ₹5,000 a month. His friends said — 'Itne mein kya hoga?' He didn't argue. He just kept investing.
2008 crash. Market down 50%. Everyone pulled out. Ravi didn't. His wife asked him to stop. He said — 'This is when it matters most.'
For 15 years, nothing dramatic happened. He didn't buy a fancy car. Didn't take international vacations. He just kept putting in ₹5,000. Then ₹7,000. Then ₹10,000.
2024. Ravi checks his portfolio. ₹2.1 crore. He didn't earn it in a day. He earned it in 7,300 days. Compound interest isn't exciting. Until it is.
₹5,000/month at 12% for 20 years = ₹49 lakhs. For 25 years = ₹94 lakhs. For 30 years = ₹1.76 crore. The only variable? Time. Start now.

episodes.synopsis: A man earning ₹30,000/month starts investing ₹5000 in SIPs at 25. Everyone laughed. At 45, he was worth ₹2 crore. The math isn't magic — it's patience.
episodes.caption: He earned ₹30,000/month. No inheritance. No lottery. Just ₹5,000 and patience. Would you have the discipline to not touch it for 20 years? 💬

episodes.title: One Hospital Bill

slides.text: They had a 3BHK in Pune. Two cars. Annual Goa trips. Combined income — ₹1.5 lakh/month. They thought they were set.
March 15. Suresh, 44, collapsed at his office. Heart attack. Rushed to a private hospital. Surgery that night. He survived. Their finances didn't.
Angioplasty + ICU + 8 days admission = ₹12,40,000. Health insurance? None. 'We never thought we'd need it,' she said. They were paying ₹45,000/month in EMIs. But not ₹1,500/month for insurance.
Savings — gone in a week. Credit card maxed. Personal loan at 16% interest. Then the car EMI bounced. Then the home loan EMI bounced. CIBIL score crashed.
They sold one car. Moved to a 2BHK. Took 3 years to recover. All because they saved ₹1,500/month by not buying health insurance. The most expensive saving of their lives.
A ₹10 lakh health insurance policy costs ₹12,000-18,000/year. That's ₹1,000-1,500/month. Less than your Netflix + Swiggy bill. Get. Insured.

episodes.synopsis: A middle-class family with two incomes, a nice flat, and zero health insurance. One heart attack. ₹12 lakh bill. Savings wiped. EMIs defaulted. Life changed in 48 hours.
episodes.caption: ₹1.5 lakh/month income. Zero health insurance. One heart attack changed everything. Do you have health insurance? Be honest 👇

episodes.title: The EMI Trap

slides.text: Amit, 28, software engineer, ₹80,000/month. His parents said — 'Beta, pehle ghar lo.' So he did. ₹50 lakh flat. ₹45 lakh loan. EMI: ₹38,000/month.
₹38,000 EMI × 240 months = ₹91,20,000. He'd pay ₹91 lakh for a ₹50 lakh flat. Almost double. But nobody thinks about the total. They only ask — 'EMI kitni hai?'
Year 2. Wife pregnant. Year 3. Father's knee surgery. Year 4. Company downsized — 3 months without salary. EMI doesn't care about your problems. It shows up every month.
He couldn't quit his toxic job — EMI. Couldn't start a business — EMI. Couldn't move cities for a better opportunity — EMI. The flat was his. But his life wasn't.
Rent for the same flat? ₹15,000/month. He'd have saved ₹23,000/month. Invested in SIPs for 10 years, that's ₹55+ lakhs. And he'd still have freedom. Buying isn't always winning.

episodes.synopsis: Amit bought a ₹50 lakh flat on loan at 28. The EMI was 'manageable.' Then life happened — job loss, wife's pregnancy, parents' medical bills. The flat became a prison.
episodes.caption: ₹38,000 EMI for 20 years. He paid ₹91 lakh for a ₹50 lakh flat. And lost his freedom along the way. Is buying a house always the right move? 🤔

episodes.title: The LIC Lie

slides.text: Your parents bought an LIC endowment plan in 1998. Agent uncle said — 'Tax bachega, insurance milega, paisa bhi badhega.' Three benefits in one. Sounds perfect, right?
Premium: ₹5,000/month. Duration: 25 years. Total paid: ₹15,00,000. Maturity amount: ₹25,00,000. Return: ₹10 lakh profit. Your parents were happy. But should they be?
₹15 lakh over 25 years returning ₹25 lakh = 4-5% annual return. Inflation in India? 6-7%. Your parents' money grew slower than prices. In real terms, they lost purchasing power.
Same ₹5,000/month in a simple index fund for 25 years at 12%? ₹94 lakh. Plus a ₹1 crore term insurance policy for ₹800/month. Better insurance AND better returns. Exposed.
LIC agents earn 25-35% commission in year one. On your ₹60,000 annual premium, the agent pockets ₹15,000-21,000. No wonder they push it so hard. It's not advice — it's sales.
Insurance and investment are two different things. Never mix them. Term insurance for protection. SIP/PPF for growth. That's it. Tell your parents.

episodes.synopsis: Your parents paid ₹5,000/month into LIC for 25 years. Total paid: ₹15 lakhs. Maturity amount: ₹25 lakhs. Sounds great? After inflation, they actually lost money.
episodes.caption: Your parents paid ₹15 lakh to LIC over 25 years. Got back ₹25 lakh. Sounds great — until you do the real math. Share this with your family before they renew that policy 👇

episodes.title: Gold Ka Chakkar

slides.text: Indian households own 25,000 tonnes of gold. More than the USA, Germany, and Switzerland's reserves combined. We love gold like no one else. But here's the thing — it hasn't made us rich.
Gold isn't investment in India. It's insurance. It's 'beti ki shaadi.' It's 'bure waqt ke liye.' It's emotion stored in a locker. And emotion is a terrible financial advisor.

Gold returns over 30 years: ~8-9% per year. Nifty 50 returns over 30 years: ~15-16% per year. ₹1 lakh in gold in 1994 = ₹10 lakh today. Same ₹1 lakh in Nifty = ₹80+ lakh. That's not a small difference.
Buy gold jewelry? 10-25% making charges gone on day one. Sell it back? 10-20% less than market price. You lose 20-40% in the round trip. That's not investing. That's donating to the jeweler.
Want gold exposure? Buy Sovereign Gold Bonds. No making charges. 2.5% annual interest on top. Tax-free at maturity. You get gold returns without the jewelry trap. Your nani doesn't need to know.

episodes.synopsis: Indian households hold more gold than the reserves of USA, Germany, and Switzerland combined. Yet most middle-class families with gold aren't wealthy. Gold is emotion, not investment.
episodes.caption: India owns more gold than most countries' reserves. But gold jewelry isn't investment — it's emotion with making charges. How much gold does your family have sitting in a locker? 👇

episodes.title: Minimum Due

slides.text: Neha got her first credit card at 24. ₹2 lakh limit. 'It's free money,' she joked. She wasn't joking for long.
Month 1: ₹15,000. Month 2: ₹22,000. Month 3: Diwali shopping — ₹40,000. Total outstanding: ₹80,000. But the minimum due said: ₹4,000. 'That's manageable,' she thought.

Credit card interest: 36-42% per year. Not 12%. Not 15%. Thirty. Six. Percent. On ₹80,000, that's ₹2,400/month just in interest. Her ₹4,000 minimum payment barely covered interest. The principal? Almost untouched.

She kept using the card. Kept paying minimum. After 3 years, she'd paid ₹1.5 lakh in minimum payments. Her outstanding balance? ₹2.4 lakh. She paid more than the original amount and owed MORE than before.
She took a personal loan at 12% to pay off the credit card at 36%. Saved ₹20,000/month in interest. Took 18 months to clear everything. Now she pays her full credit card bill. Every. Single. Month.
Credit card rule: If you can't pay the full amount this month, you can't afford it. Minimum due isn't a feature. It's a trap designed to keep you paying forever.

episodes.synopsis: Pay the minimum due on your credit card and sleep peacefully. That's what Neha thought. 3 years later, her ₹80,000 shopping bill had become ₹2.4 lakhs.
episodes.caption: ₹80,000 bill. Paid ₹1.5 lakh in minimums. Still owed ₹2.4 lakh. Credit card interest is 36%. Do you pay your full bill every month? 💳

episodes.title: PPF — The Boring Millionaire Maker

slides.text: Everyone's chasing crypto, options trading, the next multibagger. Meanwhile, the most reliable wealth-building tool in India has been sitting in a post office since 1968. It's called PPF. And it's criminally underrated.
₹500/month to ₹1.5 lakh/year. 7.1% interest, compounded yearly. 15-year lock-in. Tax-free at every stage — investment (80C), interest, and maturity. Triple tax benefit. Nothing else gives you this.
₹12,500/month (₹1.5L/year) for 15 years. You put in: ₹22.5 lakh. You get back: ₹40.68 lakh. That's ₹18 lakh in interest. Tax-free. Guaranteed. No market risk.
But here's the secret. After 15 years, you can extend in 5-year blocks. Keep adding ₹1.5L/year. After 25 years? ₹1.03 crore. After 30 years? ₹1.54 crore. All tax-free.
PPF won't make you rich overnight. It won't give you a story for parties. But in 25 years, while everyone who chased quick money is still chasing it — you'll be done. Boring wins.

episodes.synopsis: PPF. 15-year lock-in. 7.1% interest. Sounds boring. But ₹1.5 lakh/year for 15 years, extended twice, creates a tax-free corpus of ₹1 crore+.
episodes.caption: ₹12,500/month. 25 years. ₹1 crore. Tax-free. Government guaranteed. No risk. PPF is the most boring — and most reliable — wealth tool in India. Have you opened one yet? 👇

episodes.title: The Wedding Gift

slides.text: In 2000, little Arjun was born. His chacha gave a gift. Not gold. Not clothes. He invested ₹50,000 in a mutual fund in Arjun's name. Everyone thought it was a weird gift.
The parents put the papers in a drawer and forgot. No one checked. No one tracked. The money just sat there. Growing. Silently. For 24 years.
2024. Arjun, now 24, finds old papers while cleaning. Takes them to the bank. The advisor checks the system. Pauses. Checks again. '₹18,42,000.' From ₹50,000.
₹50,000 at ~16% CAGR for 24 years = ₹18+ lakh. That's 36x growth. No additional investment. No monitoring. Just time doing what time does.
Next time there's a baby in your family — skip the gold chain. Open a mutual fund. ₹50,000 today could be their first car, their education fund, or their startup capital. Be that chacha.

episodes.synopsis: In 2000, an uncle gifted a newborn ₹50,000 invested in a mutual fund. The parents forgot about it. When the kid turned 24, it was worth ₹18 lakh.
episodes.caption: ₹50,000 in 2000. ₹18 lakh in 2024. No additional investment. Just time. What's the best financial gift you've ever received? 👇

episodes.title: Auto Wale Bhaiya

slides.text: Ramesh drives an auto in Lucknow. Earns ₹18,000-22,000/month. He has no degree. No financial advisor. But his money game is better than most software engineers I know.
₹3,000/month in PPF. ₹1,500/month in his daughter's Sukanya Samriddhi account. ₹500/month term insurance. Total: ₹5,000/month. 25% of his income. Invested before he spends.
'YouTube pe sab hai, bhaiya,' he told me. 'Ek finance wala channel dekha. Samajh aa gaya. Insurance alag, investment alag. Simple hai.' He doesn't know the term 'financial literacy.' He just has it.
Meanwhile — a techie earning ₹1.2 lakh/month. No insurance. No investments. ₹40,000 EMI, ₹15,000 on food delivery, ₹8,000 on subscriptions. 'Savings? Next month se karunga.'
Financial literacy isn't about income. It's about behavior. Ramesh will retire with ₹35-40 lakh. Tax-free. The techie might retire with loans. Earning more doesn't mean keeping more.

episodes.synopsis: A Lucknow auto driver earning ₹800/day has term insurance, a PPF account, and his daughter in a good school. No MBA. Just common sense and YouTube.
episodes.caption: An auto driver with ₹20K/month income has better finances than most people earning ₹1 lakh+. Income isn't the problem. Behavior is. What's your excuse? 👇

episodes.title: Shaadi Ka Kharcha

slides.text: Indian average wedding cost: ₹12-15 lakh. That's more than most people's annual salary. And half of it goes to impressing people who won't remember the food next week.
Priya's family budget: ₹10 lakh. Actual cost: ₹15 lakh. Gap: ₹5 lakh. Solution: Personal loan at 14%. 'It's just ₹12,000/month for 5 years,' the bank said. Just.
₹12,000 × 60 months = ₹7,18,000. They borrowed ₹5 lakh. Paid back ₹7.18 lakh. That extra ₹2.18 lakh? Interest. The most expensive DJ and flower decoration ever.

₹5 lakh invested instead of borrowed = ₹9.3 lakh in 5 years at 12%. The real cost of that loan wasn't ₹2.18 lakh in interest. It was ₹2.18 lakh PLUS ₹4.3 lakh in missed returns. Total damage: ₹6.5 lakh.
No one remembers your wedding menu after a month. No one cares about the flower arrangements. They remember if they had fun. And fun doesn't cost ₹15 lakh. Cut the guest list. Keep the marriage.

episodes.synopsis: ₹15 lakh wedding. ₹10 lakh from savings, ₹5 lakh personal loan. The marriage lasted. But the loan took 5 years to pay off.
episodes.caption: ₹5 lakh loan for a wedding = ₹7.18 lakh repaid. Plus ₹4.3 lakh in missed returns. That's ₹6.5 lakh for one night. Worth it? 👇

episodes.title: Salary Account Secrets

slides.text: Your salary account has at least 5 benefits you've never claimed. Free personal accident insurance. Discounted locker fees. Better FD rates. Banks don't tell you. Because informed customers cost them money.
Most salary accounts with HDFC, ICICI, SBI come with free personal accident insurance — ₹5-20 lakh. You're already covered. You just never checked. Open your banking app right now.
Salary account holders get 0.25-0.5% higher FD rates at most banks. On ₹5 lakh for 1 year, that's ₹2,500 extra. Free. Just for asking.
Salary account = pre-approved credit cards with lower interest rates. But here's the real move — ask for a fee waiver on annual charges. They almost always say yes for salary accounts.
Banks NEED salary accounts. It's guaranteed monthly deposits. You have leverage. Negotiate locker fees. Ask for zero-charge demand drafts. You're not begging. They need you.

episodes.synopsis: Your salary account has benefits you've never used. Free insurance, better FD rates, locker discounts. Banks don't advertise these because they profit when you don't ask.
episodes.caption: Your salary account has benefits worth ₹10,000-50,000/year that you've never claimed. Check your banking app tonight. What hidden benefit did you find? 👇

episodes.title: The Disappearing ₹500

slides.text: In 2000, your dad handed you ₹500. You felt rich. Movie tickets: ₹60. Dinner for 4: ₹200. Auto home: ₹30. Change left over. Today, ₹500 gets you one Starbucks coffee and regret.
Petrol 2000: ₹28/litre. Now: ₹105. Milk 2000: ₹14/litre. Now: ₹60. Movie ticket 2000: ₹30. Now: ₹300. Your salary went up 3x. Prices went up 4x.
Inflation at 7% means your money loses half its value in 10 years. That ₹10 lakh in your savings account? In 10 years, it buys what ₹5 lakh buys today.
Your savings account gives 3-4% interest. Inflation is 6-7%. Your money in a savings account is losing 2-3% every year. The bank is thanking you for the free loan.
Beat inflation with: Equity (12-15%). PPF (7.1% tax-free). Even FDs beat savings accounts. The goal isn't to earn more. It's to ensure your money doesn't shrink while it sits.

episodes.synopsis: In 2000, ₹500 bought a family dinner, a movie, and an auto ride home. In 2024, it barely covers two coffees. Inflation is your life getting more expensive every day.
episodes.caption: ₹500 in 2000 = family outing. ₹500 in 2024 = one coffee. If your money isn't growing faster than 7% per year, you're getting poorer. What did ₹500 buy when you were a kid? 👇

episodes.title: The SIP That Saved a Family

slides.text: Manoj, 38, government school teacher. ₹25,000/month salary. Never talked about money. Died in a road accident in 2022. Left behind a wife, a 12-year-old son, and a secret.
Kavita had no income. ₹40,000 in savings. Relatives offered sympathy, not money. She found Manoj's papers while sorting his things. Mutual fund letters. She didn't understand any of it.
She took the papers to the bank. The advisor looked up the account. 'Ma'am, your husband had a SIP running for 8 years. ₹3,000 per month. Current value: ₹6,41,000.' She broke down.
That ₹6.4 lakh paid for her son's school fees for 4 years. It bought time. Time to find a job. Manoj never talked about it. He just set up the SIP and let it run. Every month. Silently.
You don't need to earn a lot. You need to automate a little. ₹3,000/month. Set it and forget it. You might not be around to see it help. But the people you love will be.

episodes.synopsis: After her husband's sudden death, Kavita had nothing — except a SIP he'd silently been running for 8 years. ₹3,000/month. Value: ₹6.4 lakh. It paid for her son's education.
episodes.caption: A school teacher earning ₹25,000/month. A silent SIP of ₹3,000. 8 years later, it saved his family. Do you have a SIP running? If not, set one up tonight. 👇

episodes.title: The Retirement Number

slides.text: ₹1 crore. Say it out loud. Feels like a lot, right? Retire with ₹1 crore and live like a king. That's the dream. Here's why the dream is broken.
Monthly expenses today: ₹50,000. Retire at 55. Life expectancy: 80. That's 25 years. ₹50,000 × 12 × 25 = ₹1.5 crore. Already short. And we haven't even added inflation yet.
₹50,000/month today at 6% inflation = ₹1,60,000/month in 20 years. Same lifestyle. Same expenses. But 3x the cost. Your ₹1 crore won't even last 8 years at that rate.
To retire at 55 with ₹50K/month lifestyle, you need ₹5-7 crore. Not ₹1 crore. Five to seven. That sounds scary. But it's not impossible. It just means you start NOW.
₹15,000/month from age 25 at 12% = ₹7 crore at 55. That's it. One SIP. 30 years. No lottery needed. Just boring consistency. Start today. Not Monday. Today.

episodes.synopsis: Everyone says '₹1 crore is enough to retire.' At 6% inflation and ₹50,000/month expenses, ₹1 crore lasts exactly 11 years. Then what?
episodes.caption: ₹1 crore isn't enough to retire. At ₹50K/month expenses and 6% inflation, you need ₹5-7 crore. Scary? It's actually just ₹15K/month started at 25. When did you start? 👇

episodes.title: Broker Ka Commission

slides.text: You bought a flat for ₹65 lakh. Sold it 7 years later for ₹80 lakh. ₹15 lakh profit. You felt like a genius. Then the deductions started.
Broker: 2% = ₹1.6 lakh. Stamp duty + registration: ₹4.5 lakh. Maintenance + property tax: ₹3.5 lakh. Capital gains tax: ₹1.5 lakh. Total costs: ₹11.1 lakh.
₹15 lakh - ₹11.1 lakh = ₹3.9 lakh actual profit. Over 7 years. That's ₹4,600/month. Your 'investment' earned less than a savings account.
Your broker showed the flat 3 times. Took maybe 5 hours total. Made ₹1.6 lakh. That's ₹32,000/hour. You held the property for 7 years and made ₹3.9 lakh.
Real estate isn't automatically a great investment. After all costs, many properties barely beat FDs. The real money in real estate? Ask the broker. They always win.

episodes.synopsis: You sold your flat for ₹80 lakh. Profit: ₹15 lakh. After broker, taxes, stamp duty — actual profit: ₹3.9 lakh in 7 years.
episodes.caption: Sold a flat for ₹80 lakh. Thought I made ₹15 lakh. After all costs — ₹3.9 lakh in 7 years. The broker made more per hour than I did. Who really makes money in real estate? 👇

episodes.title: Ghar Mein Cash

slides.text: Your mom has cash hidden in a steel almirah. Between the sarees. In a Bournvita dabba. You think it's old-fashioned. But she's been through things your UPI app hasn't.
2016: Demonetization. ATMs empty for weeks. 2020: Lockdown. Banks had limited hours. 2023: UPI server down for 6 hours. Every time, the people with cash at home slept fine.
But. ₹5 lakh in cash loses ₹35,000/year to inflation. No interest. No growth. Theft risk. Fire risk. It's the most expensive way to store money.
Smart middle ground? ₹20,000-50,000 in cash at home. Enough for 1-2 weeks of emergencies. Rest in a liquid fund or savings account. Peace of mind AND growth.
Your parents aren't foolish with money. They're cautious from experience. The generation that survived bank failures and currency changes has earned the right to keep some cash. Just not all of it.

episodes.synopsis: Your parents have ₹2-5 lakh in cash at home. You judge them. But they survived demonetization, bank server crashes, and UPI outages.
episodes.caption: Your mom's cash in the almirah isn't foolish — it's experience. But ₹5 lakh in cash loses ₹35,000/year. How much cash does your family keep at home? (No judgment) 👇

episodes.title: February Ka Panic

slides.text: February. HR sends the tax declaration email. Suddenly every salaried Indian becomes a financial expert. 'PPF mein daal do.' 'ELSS le lo.' Panic investing. The worst kind.
Mistake 1: Buying LIC for 'tax saving.' You save ₹46,800 in tax. You lose ₹4-5 lakh in returns over 20 years. Mistake 2: Not knowing your EPF already covers ₹1.8 lakh of 80C.
EPF: Already being deducted. PPF: ₹500-12,500/month. ELSS: Best tax-saving + return combo. 3-year lock-in. That's it. Three instruments. Done by April.
NPS: Extra ₹50,000 deduction under 80CCD(1B). Health insurance: ₹25,000 under 80D. Home loan interest: ₹2 lakh under Section 24. Together: ₹80,000+ in tax saved.
Set it up in April. Automate the SIPs. Forget about it. Next February, while everyone's panicking, you're done. Tax planning in April takes 1 hour. Tax panic in February costs lakhs.

episodes.synopsis: Every February, salaried Indians panic-buy the worst financial products for tax saving. This rush costs them lakhs over a lifetime.
episodes.caption: Every February, India panic-buys the worst financial products. Set up tax saving in April. 1 hour of planning saves lakhs. When do you do your tax planning? 👇

episodes.title: UPI Scam Season

slides.text: Rohit, 29, Bangalore. Got a call: 'Sir, your KYC is expiring. Your account will be frozen in 2 hours.' He panicked. 4 minutes later, ₹2,30,000 was gone.
The scammer knew Rohit's name, bank, and last 4 digits. Sent a 'verification link' on WhatsApp. Rohit clicked. Entered his UPI PIN. Done. The scammer didn't break in. Rohit opened the door.
Called the bank in 10 minutes. Too late. Called cyber crime helpline 1930. Filed FIR. After 3 months, got back ₹87,000. Not even half.
No bank calls about KYC. Ever. UPI PIN is for SENDING money, not receiving. If someone creates urgency — it's a scam. Urgency is their weapon.
2023: Indians lost ₹10,319 crore to digital fraud. 30% increase from 2022. Your only defense? Slow down. Hang up. Verify.

episodes.synopsis: A Bangalore techie lost ₹2.3 lakh in 4 minutes through a UPI scam. No hack — just a phone call and the right words.
episodes.caption: ₹2.3 lakh gone in 4 minutes. No hack — just a phone call. UPI scams increased 30% last year. Share your story to warn others 👇

episodes.title: SIP vs Lump Sum

slides.text: ₹6 lakh ready to invest. Every finance influencer says 'SIP karo.' Your broker friend says 'Lump sum.' Your dad says 'FD.' Who's right?
Historical data: Lump sum beats SIP 65% of the time over 10-year periods. Markets trend upward. By delaying, you miss early growth. But the math doesn't account for your stomach.
You invest ₹6 lakh Monday. Market drops 15% Tuesday. Your ₹6 lakh is now ₹5.1 lakh. You can't sleep. You want to sell. The math was right. Your emotions weren't ready.
Nerves of steel? Lump sum wins statistically. Can't handle drops? SIP over 3-6 months. The best investment is one you don't panic-sell.
The debate doesn't matter as much as just investing. ₹6 lakh sitting in savings at 3.5% while you debate for 6 months? That's the real loss. Decide and move.

episodes.synopsis: ₹6 lakh to invest. All at once or monthly? The answer isn't what most finance influencers tell you.
episodes.caption: SIP or Lump Sum? Data says lump sum wins 65% of the time. But data doesn't account for your panic at 2 AM. What would you do with ₹6 lakh? 👇

episodes.title: Salary Slip Decoded

slides.text: Your CTC is ₹12 lakh. Your in-hand is ₹72,000/month. Where did ₹28,000/month disappear? Let's open your salary slip.
Basic: 40-50% of CTC. HRA: 40-50% of Basic. PF: 12% from you + 12% from employer. Gratuity: 4.8% of Basic. These 'benefits' are why CTC ≠ in-hand.
Rented house? HRA exemption saves ₹50,000-1,00,000/year. Living with parents? Pay them rent, get a receipt, claim HRA. Legal. Smart. Most people miss this.
Your EPF: 12% of Basic + employer 12%. On ₹50K Basic, that's ₹12,000/month locked away. Earns 8.1%. Tax-free after 5 years. Forced saving — and it's powerful.
Read your salary slip. Once. 15 minutes. Then optimize — HRA, NPS, food coupons. ₹1-2 lakh in tax saved just by reading the fine print.

episodes.synopsis: 73% of salaried Indians don't fully understand their salary slip. CTC vs in-hand. Basic vs HRA. One slip, fully decoded.
episodes.caption: CTC ₹12 lakh. In-hand: ₹72,000. Where did the rest go? Decode yours tonight — share what you found 👇

episodes.title: Emergency Fund

slides.text: Pop quiz. Right now, if you needed ₹2 lakh in 24 hours — no salary, no borrowing — could you do it? If no, you don't have an emergency fund. 76% of Indians can't.
Job loss — 3 months to find a new one. Bike accident — ₹80,000 out of pocket. Phone call: 'Papa ki tabiyat kharab hai' — next flight home. Life doesn't send advance notice.
The rule: 6 months of expenses. Not income — expenses. Spend ₹40,000/month? You need ₹2.4 lakh accessible in 24 hours. In a liquid fund or savings account.
Start with ₹1,000/month. After your first ₹50,000, you'll feel different. After ₹1 lakh, you'll sleep different. It's not about the amount — it's about knowing it's there.
Savings account: Instant access, 3.5%. Liquid mutual fund: 1-day withdrawal, 6-7%. Sweep-in FD: Auto-converts to FD. Pick one. Fund it. Forget it.

episodes.synopsis: 76% of Indians can't handle an unexpected ₹50,000 expense. The 6-month rule and why it's the foundation of every money plan.
episodes.caption: 76% of Indians can't handle a ₹50,000 emergency. The fix: 6 months of expenses in a liquid account. How big is YOUR emergency fund? 👇

episodes.title: BNPL — The New Credit Trap

slides.text: Simpl. LazyPay. ZestMoney. 'Buy now, pay later. Zero interest.' You bought shoes for ₹3,000 you didn't need because it said 'Pay ₹1,000 × 3 months.' Felt free. It wasn't.
BNPL companies don't make money from on-time payments. They make money from late fees, interest after the free period, and your spending data. You're not the customer. You're the product.
Meera, 23, used BNPL on 7 apps. ₹2,000 here, ₹3,500 there. Month-end: ₹18,000 in BNPL dues on a ₹35,000 salary. Missed one payment. Late fee + 24% interest kicked in.
BNPL reports to CIBIL. Miss payments? Credit score drops. Future home loan? Higher interest. Credit card application? Rejected. ₹3,000 shoes just cost you lakhs.
If you can't pay for it in full right now, you can't afford it. The installment isn't making it cheaper. It's making it easier to overspend. Delete the apps.

episodes.synopsis: Buy Now Pay Later feels like free money. BNPL companies make money when you miss a payment — and they're designed to make sure you do.
episodes.caption: BNPL feels free. But late fees, interest, and CIBIL damage cost more than you think. How many BNPL apps are on your phone? Count and comment 👇

episodes.title: The 50-30-20 Reality Check

slides.text: The internet says: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings. Now try this on ₹50,000/month in Mumbai. Rent alone is ₹20,000. That's 40% gone on ONE need.
Rent: ₹20,000. Groceries: ₹8,000. Transport: ₹3,000. Bills: ₹4,000. Parents: ₹5,000. Total needs: ₹40,000. That's 80%. On NEEDS. Not wants.
Indian version: 60-20-20 or even 70-10-20. The key: savings are NON-NEGOTIABLE. Even 10%. Even ₹5,000. Pay yourself first.
Day 1 of salary: Auto-debit to SIP + PPF. Don't think. What's left is what you spend. Not the other way around. The order matters.
If you're saving 10% in an expensive city on an average salary — you're doing better than 80% of India. ₹2,000/month is a start. Not a failure.

episodes.synopsis: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings. Beautiful rule. Doesn't work on an Indian salary in Mumbai.
episodes.caption: 50-30-20 doesn't work for most Indians. Rent alone eats 40%. The realistic rule: Save FIRST, spend what's left. What's YOUR savings percentage? 👇

episodes.title: Same Salary, Different Life

slides.text: Arun and Vikram. Same team. Same ₹60,000/month. Arun is broke by the 20th. Vikram invested ₹1.5 lakh this year AND went to Goa. Same money. Different lives. Why?
Salary day: Zomato celebration ₹800. New sneakers ₹4,500. Weekend pub ₹3,000. Amazon at 2 AM ₹2,200. By day 10, ₹15,000 gone on 'small things.' By day 20, borrowing from Vikram.
Salary day: Auto-debit — ₹10,000 SIP, ₹5,000 PPF. Remaining: ₹45,000. Rent: ₹15,000. Bills: ₹12,000. Fun: ₹10,000 (guilt-free). Travel fund: ₹5,000. Buffer: ₹3,000.
Arun spends first, saves what's left (nothing). Vikram saves first, spends what's left (guilt-free). Same money. Different order. That's the entire secret.
Set up one auto-debit SIP today. Even ₹5,000. Then spend whatever's left without guilt. That's freedom. Not the next salary hike.

episodes.title: The One Rule

slides.text: 24 episodes. SIPs, LIC traps, credit card debt, emergency funds, BNPL, real estate, salary slips. Lots of rules. But there's only ONE rule that matters.
Spend less than you earn. Invest the difference. Repeat until you die. That's it. That's the entire personal finance industry in one sentence.
Ramesh the auto driver did it on ₹20,000. Ravi the SIP guy did it on ₹30,000. Manoj the teacher did it on ₹25,000. None were rich. All were disciplined. Income doesn't build wealth. Behavior does.
Open your phone. Set up a ₹1,000 SIP. Not next month. RIGHT NOW. The best time was 10 years ago. The second best time is today.
This series gave you stories. Not advice. What you do with them is up to you. 10 years from now, you'll either be the person who started — or the one who wished they had. Choose.
